items.prompt: Explain the link between choosing a suitable instrument and obtaining a useful experimental reading.
items.canonical_answer: Its range and scale must suit the expected quantity. Correct arrangement and reading then allow the intended value, rather than an accidental artefact, to be measured.
marking_guidance: Credit 1 (1): Instrument range/resolution suited to quantity.
Credit 2 (1): Correct setup/reading makes the result represent that quantity; require the link, not just two instrument names.

Maximum 2 marks. Accept equivalent scientifically correct wording or a labelled representation of the same points. Count each distinct idea once; an unsupported keyword alone is not a causal explanation.
The link must include a reason or result connecting the stated ideas; unrelated facts do not earn explanation credit.

items.prompt: Describe one reading action that reduces parallax when reading a graduated scale.
items.canonical_answer: The eye is level with the reading, with its sight line perpendicular to the scale.

Accepted alternative wording: “at right angles” for “perpendicular”. The stated directions, quantities and conditions are still required.

items.prompt: Explain the distinction between the independent variable and a control in a cooling investigation.
items.canonical_answer: The independent variable is intentionally changed to test its effect. A relevant control is held fixed so it does not provide a competing explanation for the measured change.
marking_guidance: Credit 1 (1): Independent variable intentionally changed.
Credit 2 (1): Control held fixed to exclude a competing cause.

Maximum 2 marks. Accept equivalent scientifically correct wording or a labelled representation of the same points. Count each distinct idea once; an unsupported keyword alone is not a causal explanation.

items.prompt: An experiment varies the time for which a heater operates and measures water temperature. Explain which quantity is independent, distinguishing it from the response.
items.canonical_answer: Heating duration is independent because it is deliberately varied. Water temperature is the measured response rather than the chosen setting.
marking_guidance: Credit 1 (1): Heating time identified as deliberately changed.
Credit 2 (1): Temperature identified as measured response.

Maximum 2 marks. Accept equivalent scientifically correct wording or a labelled representation of the same points. Count each distinct idea once; an unsupported keyword alone is not a causal explanation.

items.canonical_answer: A starting-temperature difference could change the cooling behaviour independently of the surface. Keeping it matched makes the surface comparison more meaningful.

Credit 2 (1): Matching them isolates surface finish.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: test water temperature as heating time increases at a fixed heater setting. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter. 

| Heating time / s | Temperature / °C |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 22 |
| 30 | 24.4 |
| 60 | 26.8 |
| 90 | 29.2 |
| 120 | 31.6 |
| 150 | 34 |

(a) Draw Temperature / °C vertically against Heating time / s horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to test water temperature as heating time increases at a fixed heater setting. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Temperature / °C is vertical and Heating time / s horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (0, 22) and (150, 34). Gradient = (34 − 22) / (150 − 0) = 0.08 °C/s. The slope is temperature rise per second, 0.08 °C/s. For 0.100 kg of water with c = 4200 J/(kg K), the water gains energy at mc(dT/dt) = 33.6 W. A roughly 35 W heater allows about 1.4 W for losses in this idealised example; voltage alone does not set its power.

Arrangement: A 6 V immersion heater rated about 35 W, a suitably rated current-limited 6 V supply and leads, 0.100 kg water in an insulated beaker, thermometer, stirrer and stopwatch

Plan: 1. Weigh 0.100 kg of water into the insulated beaker and immerse the 6 V, approximately 35 W heater before switching it on. 2. Place the thermometer in the water away from the heater and beaker wall and record initial temperature. 3. Start the stopwatch with heating and maintain the same supply voltage and heater setting. 4. Stir gently and record temperature every 30 s for 150 s without removing the thermometer. 5. Repeat with fresh water at the same starting temperature and record all repeats.
Control and accuracy: Keep heater power and water mass fixed; stir gently for a representative water temperature and handle hot apparatus safely.
Table: Heating time / s; Temperature / °C; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The temperature-time gradient gives the warming rate. Convert to power only when water mass and specific heat capacity are included and heat losses/container heating are allowed for.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-2.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit °C/s or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).

(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A 6 V immersion heater rated about 35 W, a suitably rated current-limited 6 V supply and leads, 0.100 kg water in an insulated beaker, thermometer, stirrer and stopwatch

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Place the thermometer in the water away from the heater and beaker wall and record initial temperature.; Stir gently and record temperature every 30 s for 150 s without removing the thermometer.; Repeat with fresh water at the same starting temperature and record all repeats.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Keep heater power and water mass fixed; stir gently for a representative water temperature and handle hot apparatus safely.
(c) Table (1): Heating time / s; Temperature / °C; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The temperature-time gradient gives the warming rate. Convert to power only when water mass and specific heat capacity are included and heat losses/container heating are allowed for.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. Proposed teaching rubric, not a reconstructed official mark scheme.
